19 OCTOBER 2026 · LEE C. STONEHOUSE

The brain burns a fifth of resting energy on two percent of body mass. Its fastest buffer is phosphocreatine.

Creatine Is a Brain Supplement: The Phosphate Buffer Your Head Runs Out of First

Ask most people about creatine and they will describe a gym supplement: bigger lifts, water weight, bodybuilding. That framing undersells it badly. Creatine's real job is energy buffering, and the organ that leans on that buffer hardest is not a muscle in your arms or legs. It is your brain.

THE FASTEST ENERGY SYSTEM YOU HAVE

Your body has three energy systems. The aerobic system runs on oxygen and takes minutes. The glycolytic system burns carbohydrate and takes tens of seconds. The fastest is the phosphagen system: a molecule called phosphocreatine sits inside every energy-hungry cell and instantly hands its phosphate group to ADP, regenerating ATP, the cell's energy currency, in a fraction of a second.

Phosphocreatine is not fuel for the marathon. It is the surge tank. It covers the first five to ten seconds of near-maximal effort, and then takes minutes to refill. Every hard sprint, every heavy single, every explosive movement draws on it first.

The same machinery runs in the brain. The brain is roughly two percent of body mass but consumes around twenty percent of resting energy, and it has no meaningful fuel reserves of its own. When demand spikes, the phosphocreatine buffer is what keeps ATP supply matched to demand in the seconds between one energy cycle and the next.

WHAT CHANGES AFTER 40

Brain phosphocreatine concentration declines with age, and the brain becomes more vulnerable to energy shortfalls: slower cognitive recovery after effort, less resilience under sleep deprivation, greater sensitivity to metabolic stress. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy studies have shown that creatine supplementation raises brain creatine concentrations measurably, and that the effect is larger in older adults than in younger ones.

This is the honest, interesting claim: creatine is not primarily a muscle supplement that happens to be brain-safe. It is an energy-buffer supplement that happens to be famous for gym use. The brain application and the muscle application run on the identical molecule.

WHAT THE RESEARCH ACTUALLY SHOWS

The evidence splits cleanly into three tiers, and it is worth being precise about which tier a claim sits in.

Tier one: brain creatine rises with supplementation. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy work, including Rae and colleagues' 2003 study in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, showed measurable increases in brain phosphocreatine and creatine after supplementation, with the largest responses in people whose diets contained little meat or fish. This is well established.

Tier two: cognitive effects under stress. The most consistent human finding is that creatine helps the brain cope when energy demand outruns supply: sleep deprivation, mental fatigue, demanding cognitive tasks. Rae's original work reported improvements in working memory and general cognitive performance, strongest in vegetarians. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in Nutrition Reviews (Forbes and colleagues) found the clearest benefits in these stressed or depleted states, with more modest and inconsistent effects in rested, well-fed people. In other words: creatine does not raise a rested brain above its ceiling. It raises the floor.

Tier three: general cognitive enhancement in healthy, rested adults. The evidence here is mixed to weak. If a marketing page promises creatine will make a well-rested 40-year-old measurably smarter, it is outrunning the data.

There is also a growing sleep-deprivation literature. Small trials have found that a single high dose of creatine before a night of sleep loss reduced the metabolic and cognitive toll, an effect consistent with the buffering mechanism. Promising, early, and worth following rather than treating as settled.

Phosphocreatine hands its phosphate to ADP to regenerate ATP in milliseconds. The brain leans on that transaction hardest.

THE BLOOD TEST MOST PEOPLE MISREAD

Here is a genuinely useful practical detail that almost nobody mentions: creatine supplementation raises serum creatinine on a standard blood panel.

Creatinine is a waste product of creatine breakdown, and it is the marker doctors use to estimate kidney function. Supplementation pushes it up a little, which can look like an alarming kidney flag on a routine blood test when the kidneys are working perfectly. The usual clinical check, cystatin C or a creatinine clearance estimate, sorts it out, but only if you tell the clinician you take creatine.

This matters inside a biomarker-tracking program. A marker that moves for a benign reason still needs interpreting correctly, and the way you interpret it is to know your own inputs. It is the same principle as the multivitamin argument: measure, understand what a change means, then act.

THE MUSCLE AND BONE PICTURE FOR OVER-50s

The muscle evidence is the strongest tier of all: creatine plus resistance training produces modest but reliable gains in lean mass and strength performance compared with training alone, and the effect extends to older adults. Meta-analyses that pool creatine-plus-training trials in people over fifty consistently show the combination outperforming training alone.

The bone story is more cautious. Some early work suggested creatine might help bone mineral density when combined with training in postmenopausal women, but the larger pooled analyses have not confirmed a meaningful effect on femoral neck density beyond what training itself delivers. The muscle case is solid. The bone case is not.

HOW IT IS ACTUALLY USED

The common maintenance dose is three to five grams a day. The brain literature, because brain tissue loads slowly, has often used higher doses or longer loading periods, typically around ten grams a day for several weeks in older-adult studies. Two honest caveats: the response varies between individuals, and anyone considering supplementation, particularly with a kidney condition or on relevant medication, should discuss it with their GP first.

Monohydrate is the form with the deepest evidence base and the lowest cost. The exotic alternatives have not beaten it in head-to-head trials.

TEST, TARGET, RETEST

Lee C. Stonehouse's 10-Tenet operating system treats creatine the way it treats everything else: as an intervention that has to earn its place through measurement. Biomarkers come first, interventions follow the data, and the follow-up test verifies whether the change did anything.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS

Does creatine improve memory?

The clearest effects appear when the brain is under stress: sleep deprivation, mental fatigue or heavy cognitive load. Rae and colleagues found working-memory improvements, strongest in people eating little meat. In rested, well-fed adults the evidence for general cognitive enhancement is mixed to weak. Creatine raises the floor, not the ceiling.

How long does creatine take to reach the brain?

Brain tissue loads slowly compared with muscle. Muscle responds within days, while the brain studies that measured increases in phosphocreatine typically ran for several weeks at around ten grams a day in older adults. Expect weeks, not days, if the target is brain concentration.

Is creatine safe for the kidneys?

In healthy people, the evidence does not show kidney harm at normal doses. Creatine supplementation does raise serum creatinine, the standard kidney marker, which can look like a flag on a blood test without indicating damage. Tell your clinician if you take it; alternative markers such as cystatin C clarify the picture.

Should vegetarians take creatine?

Dietary creatine comes mainly from meat and fish, so people eating little of either start with lower muscle and brain stores, and the trials show the largest responses in that group. Whether to supplement is an individual decision best made with a professional who can assess the whole picture.

What type of creatine should be used?

Creatine monohydrate has the largest evidence base, the lowest cost and the longest safety record. Newer forms have not demonstrated superiority in controlled comparisons. The dose matters more than the branding: three to five grams daily for maintenance is the common starting point.

SUMMARY · THE SHORT VERSION

Creatine's real role is energy buffering, and the brain is the organ that leans on that buffer hardest. Supplementation measurably raises brain phosphocreatine, especially in older adults and people eating little meat. The clearest cognitive benefits appear under stress: sleep loss, fatigue, heavy load. In rested, healthy adults the gains are modest. Creatine also raises serum creatinine on blood tests, which needs interpreting correctly. Muscle benefits with training are well supported; bone-density claims are not.
